query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermomechanical processing route that refines the dual-phase (fcc/B2) lamellar microstructure in eutectic HEAs will simultaneously boost room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility by reducing lamellar spacing and improving interfacial integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with relatively coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies, having numerous internal phase boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted thermomechanical treatment—such as a hybrid rolling process (e.g., initial cryo-rolling followed by warm rolling) combined with an appropriate annealing step—to refine and homogenize the fcc/B2 lamellar structure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation under quasi-static loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined lamellar spacing and enhanced phase connectivity between the soft fcc and strong B2 phases.
generation.mechanism: Finer lamellar spacing increases the ability of the ductile fcc phase to absorb strain and promotes crack deflection or arrest at coherent interfaces with the B2 phase, while the hard B2 phase sustains high loads. Together, these effects delay microcrack initiation and propagation, thereby improving both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the conventional as-cast alloy, the processed alloy will exhibit a higher yield and ultimate tensile strength accompanied by an increase in room-temperature ductility.
generation.baseline: Eutectic HEAs with an unmodified, coarser lamellar structure where internal boundaries facilitate premature microcracking, leading to limited ductility despite adequate strength.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for eutectic HEAs having a controllable composite fcc/B2 microstructure. The effect may not manifest if the alloy composition deviates significantly from the eutectic system or if the processing parameters fail to produce a refined, well-connected lamellar architecture.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of strength and ductility enhancements is uncertain and may depend sensitively on the specifics of the thermomechanical processing and exact material composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA: one via conventional casting (baseline) and one with the proposed hybrid thermomechanical treatment (cryo-rolling followed by warm rolling and targeted annealing). Subject both sets to room-temperature tensile testing and perform microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) to measure lamellar spacing and interfacial integrity.
measurements: Crack initiation and propagation sites via fractography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility, and if microstructural analysis fails to confirm a refined and well-connected fcc/B2 lamellar structure compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
